issues.legal_issue: A conviction resting substantially on an approver’s testimony requires material corroboration, particularly when the approver has retracted a confession and is otherwise untrustworthy.
material_facts: The prosecution’s substantial evidence against the appellants was the testimony of an approver who had participated in the crime and retracted his confession before the committal court.
The approver was also involved in illicit liquor manufacture and had a bad character.
The other witnesses did not corroborate the approver on material particulars, and one witness contradicted an important part of his account.
The co-accused confessions were not safe corroboration of the approver’s testimony.
issues.conclusion: The approver’s evidence, without safe corroboration in material particulars, could not sustain the appellants’ convictions; the convictions and sentences were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 133 of the Evidence Act does not bar conviction on an accomplice’s evidence alone, but section 114(b) supports the rule of prudence that an accomplice’s evidence should be corroborated in material particulars. The need is greater where the approver has retracted a confession and is not a person of truth. The Court relied on Bhuboni Sahu v. The King and Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and conviction_depended_on_approver and approver_retracted_confession and no_material_independent_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.conviction_depended_on_approver: The prosecution’s case against the accused depended substantially on an accomplice who testified for the prosecution.
predicates.approver_retracted_confession: The testifying accomplice had retracted a confession before the committal court.
predicates.no_material_independent_corroboration: The other evidence did not independently corroborate the accomplice on material particulars.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction substantially dependent on an approver who retracted a confession and lacks material independent corroboration, the conviction is not safely sustainable.

issues.legal_issue: A co-accused’s confession is not safe corroboration of an approver when it lacks assurance of independence or was obtained without adequate safeguards before its recording.
material_facts: Two co-accused had made confessions and later retracted them; the confessions were relied on to corroborate the approver.
One co-accused was brought to the magistrate together with the approver, and the record did not establish that their accounts were independent or made without prior opportunity for concert.

For the other co-accused, the magistrate did not establish that he had been warned that he was not bound to confess and that a confession could be used against him, or that he had been given adequate time to reflect on whether to confess.
The confessions could not be tested by cross-examination.
issues.conclusion: Neither co-accused confession could safely be relied on to corroborate the approver.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 30 of the Evidence Act, a confession by a co-accused jointly tried for the same offence may be taken into consideration, but it is not proof and is weaker than evidence tested by cross-examination. A confession may lend assurance to other evidence, but one accomplice’s confession should not ordinarily be used to corroborate another without independent evidence implicating the accused; apparent agreement between confessions is less weighty where independence is not established. A person produced for confession must be free from possible police influence, given time to reflect, and told that confession is not compulsory and may be used against him. The Court relied on Bhuboni Sahu v. The King, Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Sarwan Singh v. The State of Punjab.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.co_accused_confessions_offered_as_corrob: The prosecution relied on confessions by co-accused to corroborate an accomplice’s testimony against the accused.
predicates.co_accused_confessions_lacked_independen: The record did not establish that the confessions were independently made, or showed that a confession was recorded without adequate warning and time for reflection.

issues.definition: When co-accused confessions are offered to corroborate an accomplice but lack established independence or adequate safeguards, they are not safe corroboration.

issues.legal_issue: An accused’s failure to attend a planned loan transaction does not by itself establish participation in the crime.
material_facts: The accused had arranged to obtain a loan on the day after the crime but did not attend to receive it.
The prosecution suggested that he did not attend because he had obtained money from the crime.

The Court considered this the remaining circumstance relied on by the High Court and found that, even if the accused had come by money, that did not legitimately establish his participation in the murders.
issues.conclusion: The failure to attend the planned loan transaction did not establish that the accused had participated in the crime.
issues.legal_principle: A circumstance permitting more than one explanation cannot, without a sufficient evidentiary basis, support the conclusion that the accused participated in the crime; even an inference that the accused came by money does not by itself prove participation.

predicates.accused_missed_planned_loan: The accused failed to attend a planned transaction to receive a loan after the crime.
predicates.loan_absence_is_only_remaining_circumsta: The failure to attend the loan transaction is the remaining circumstance relied on to connect the accused to the crime.

issues.definition: When an accused misses a planned loan transaction and that absence is the only remaining circumstance relied on, the absence does not establish participation in the crime.
